report.executive_summary: Civic Water Engineering must select a pump module for the water-reclamation transfer loop. All four candidates clear the policy gates of quality index at least 80 and raw defects at most 5 on the shared acceptance-run basis. Measured energy per run: P2 12 kWh, P3 52, P1 56, P4 58. P2 therefore wins the lowest-energy rule, 40 kWh ahead of runner-up P3. P2 also carries the top quality index, 97, with a single recorded defect. P4 is the only zero-defect module yet posts the highest energy, 58 kWh. Cost, delivery, maintenance and field reliability remain unverified; six open questions carry to the assurance handover.
report.figure_caption: Supporting illustration: measured energy per common acceptance run by candidate, with quality index, defect counts and gaps to winner P2; P4 carries the only zero-defect callout.

recommendation.rationale: P2 qualifies (quality 97, 1 defect) and minimizes energy at 12 kWh, 40 kWh below runner-up P3 on the shared acceptance basis; the lowest-energy rule is decisive. sections.body: Applying the two policy gates to the trusted table: P1 (quality 84, 4 defects), P2 (97, 1), P3 (80, 3) and P4 (81, 0) all qualify — no candidate is screened out. Because every module qualifies, reject_all is not applicable, and no candidate-ID tie-break is needed: energy alone decides. Under the lowest-energy rule the ranking is P2 first, then P3, P1 and P4. The quality gate is satisfied with margin by P2, comfortably by P1 and P4, and exactly at the bar by P3, so qualification is robust but not uniform.
sections.heading: Policy Screen and Qualification Ranking

sections.body: The acceptance run fixes the same flow and head duty for every module, so measured energy is directly comparable. Against winner P2 (12 kWh) the gaps are P3 +40, P1 +44 and P4 +46 kWh — P4 consumes nearly five times P2's energy. Even the closest challenger, P3, trails by 40 kWh, a margin far too large for plausible test variation on a fixed basis to close. No supplied fact supports any change to this ordering, and none of the unverified commercial items could rationally outweigh a 40-plus kWh per-run energy deficit.
sections.heading: Energy Gap Analysis on the Common Basis

sections.body: Quality and energy point in different directions. P2 pairs the best quality index (97) with a single recorded defect. P4 posts the only zero-defect record in the set, with quality 81 — the lowest of the four qualifiers — but the highest measured energy. Defect counts are raw tallies; none of the four approaches the gate of 5, so the record signals build cleanliness, not disqualification. P4's clean-build benchmark is genuinely worth tracking in future acceptance runs, even though it cannot change today's energy-led ranking on this work order.
sections.heading: Quality and Defect Record Review

sections.body: Cost, delivery, maintenance and field reliability are unverified for every candidate. Six questions carry forward: 1) Sizing — is the fixed flow/head duty representative of seasonal loop demand? 2) Justification — confirm the acceptance-run basis matches commissioning tests for all four modules. 3) Reliability — obtain field reliability data, none of which is supplied. 4) Quantify — request lifecycle cost, spares and maintenance profiles, notably for P4's zero-defect build. 5) Lead times — supplier delivery commitments are unknown. 6) Zero-risk check — verify whether the single P2 defect is cosmetic or functional before contract.
sections.heading: Open Questions for the Assurance Handover
